questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Meaning of Staffing' refers to.
questions.a: The managerial work of matching people to posts: estimating how many hands of what kind are needed, then recruiting, selecting, placing, promoting, appraising and developing employees so that every position in the structure stays occupied by a capable occupant.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Meaning of Staffing'.
questions.a: In a new enterprise it follows planning and organising; in a running one it never stops, because jobs appear and people leave.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Meaning of Staffing' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.1 (source: lebs106.txt lines 88-143 (Meaning: putting people to jobs; new and existing enterprises))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Importance of Staffing' refers to.
questions.a: Why the function is critical: it discovers competent people, raises performance by fitting the right person to the right role, secures survival through succession planning, prevents both overmanning and shortages, and lifts job satisfaction through fair assessment and reward.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Importance of Staffing'.
questions.a: Human resources are the asset that decides goal attainment; wrong people in posts waste effort and lower quality, right people drive performance.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Importance of Staffing' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.2 (source: lebs106.txt lines 144-219 (Importance; benefits i-v))

concepts.title: Staffing as Part of Human Resource Management

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Staffing as Part of Human Resource Management' refers to.
questions.a: Every manager performs staffing duties -- placing, training, motivating and caring for the people in his unit -- while large firms add a specialist human resource department whose activities run from job analysis and recruitment to grievance handling, welfare and legal defence.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Staffing as Part of Human Resource Management'.
questions.a: Staffing is both a line duty of every manager and a staff advisory role of the HR department; HRM itself evolved from labour welfare officer through personnel manager to human resource manager.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Staffing as Part of Human Resource Management' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 2.1 (source: lebs106.txt lines 220-400 (Staffing as part of HRM; specialised duties; evolution of HRM))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Steps in the Staffing Process' refers to.
questions.a: Five ordered stages: estimate the manpower needed through workload and workforce analysis, search for candidates through recruitment, choose the best through selection tests and interviews, settle the newcomers through placement and orientation, and grow them through training and development.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Steps in the Staffing Process'.
questions.a: Workload analysis says how many people of what kind are required; workforce analysis says how many are available -- together they reveal overstaffing, understaffing or the optimum.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Steps in the Staffing Process' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 3.1 (source: lebs106.txt lines 401-724 (Staffing Process i-v, workload and workforce analysis))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Recruitment and Internal Sources' refers to.
questions.a: Recruitment is the search for possible candidates and the effort to interest them in applying; its internal sources fill vacancies from within -- transfers shifting an employee sideways without changing rank or pay, and promotions moving him up to higher responsibility, status and salary.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Recruitment and Internal Sources'.
questions.a: Internal hiring motivates staff, is cheaper and more reliable since candidates are known -- but it risks inbreeding, no fresh talent, and a new enterprise cannot use it at all.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Recruitment and Internal Sources' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 4.1 (source: lebs106.txt lines 883-1120 (Recruitment; transfers and promotions; merits and limitations of internal sources))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'External Sources of Recruitment' refers to.
questions.a: The channels through which outsiders are brought in: a gate notice for casual workers, a standing list of unsolicited callers, newspaper and trade advertisements, government employment exchanges, placement agencies and management consultants, campus hiring, referrals by employees, labour contractors, television ads and job websites.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'External Sources of Recruitment'.
questions.a: Outside hiring buys wider choice, fresh talent and competitive spirit at the cost of expense, delay and some resentment among existing staff.

questions.q: Under which section is 'External Sources of Recruitment' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 4.2 (source: lebs106.txt lines 1121-1431 (External sources i-x; merits and limitations))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Selection Process and Employment Tests' refers to.
questions.a: Selection picks the best candidate from the recruitment pool through a sequence of hurdles -- preliminary screening, employment tests, a formal interview, reference and background checks, the selection decision, medical fitness, then the job offer and contract of employment -- with many eliminated at each stage.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Selection Process and Employment Tests'.
questions.a: Tests probe different qualities: intelligence for learning ability, aptitude for potential to acquire skills, trade for skills already held, personality for emotional makeup, interest for inclinations.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Selection Process and Employment Tests' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 5.1 (source: lebs106.txt lines 1432-1742 (Selection; process steps i-viii; tests a-e; accept and reject errors box))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Training, Development and Education' refers to.
questions.a: Three overlapping but distinct ideas: training sharpens the aptitudes, skills and abilities needed for a specific present job; development spans the whole growth of the individual for future roles; education builds knowledge and understanding without a narrow job focus.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Training, Development and Education'.
questions.a: Training is job-oriented and short term; development is career-oriented and ongoing, and it includes training.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Training, Development and Education' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 6.1 (source: lebs106.txt lines 1832-1920 (Training, Development and Education; difference table))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Benefits of Training and Development' refers to.
questions.a: Systematic learning beats guesswork: for the firm it lifts output in quantity and quality, prepares stand-in managers, trims absenteeism and turnover, and keeps responses ready for fast technological and economic change; for the employee it brings better skills, higher earnings, fewer accidents and greater morale.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Benefits of Training and Development'.
questions.a: Five organisational benefits and four personal benefits -- productivity, future managers, morale, adaptability on one side; skills, earnings, safety, satisfaction on the other.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Benefits of Training and Development' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 6.1 (source: lebs106.txt lines 1751-1831 (Importance of training; benefits to organisation and employee))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'On-the-Job Training Methods' refers to.
questions.a: Methods applied at the workplace while the employee actually works -- learning while doing: apprenticeship under a master worker for skilled trades, coaching where a superior guides and reviews a trainee, internship run jointly by an institute and a firm, and job rotation shifting the trainee across departments for a rounded view.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'On-the-Job Training Methods'.
questions.a: Rotation readies people for promotion and transfer; apprenticeship suits plumbers and electricians; internship pairs study with practical work.

questions.q: Under which section is 'On-the-Job Training Methods' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 6.2 (source: lebs106.txt lines 1936-2046 (On the Job Methods i-iv))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Off-the-Job Training Methods' refers to.
questions.a: Methods used away from the workplace -- learning before doing: classroom lectures and conferences for rules and procedures, films for demonstrations, case studies of real problems, computer models that simulate the job risklessly, vestibule training on real equipment in a classroom setting, and programmed instruction in graded units.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Off-the-Job Training Methods'.
questions.a: Vestibule training is the giveaway case: the firm's own machines, but off the production floor, suited to costly sophisticated equipment.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Off-the-Job Training Methods' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 6.2 (source: lebs106.txt lines 2047-2129 (Off the Job Methods i-vi, vestibule training))
